arXiv:2605.07505v2 [cs.AI] 08 Oct 2026

LiteGUI: Lightweight GUI Agents via Multi-Solution Guided Distillation and Dual-Level Reinforcement Learning

Yubin Wu ††thanks: Equal contribution.    Zicheng Cai††footnotemark:    Liping Ning    Hua Wang Affiliation: Zhi Chen    Yaohua Tang ††thanks: Corresponding author. tangyaohua28@gmail.com    Hao Chen Affiliation: Moore Threads AI
Abstract

We present LiteGUI, a new framework for building lightweight GUI agents. GUI interaction poses unique challenges due to the long-horizon nature of complex tasks and the existence of multiple valid interaction paths, which are difficult for lightweight GUI agents to handle effectively. To address these challenges, LiteGUI introduces a two-stage post-training framework operating on logged GUI states. First, we propose Guided On-Policy Distillation, which provides training-time privileged teacher guidance at each GUI state by selecting the most-matched valid action from human-verified multi-solution action annotations, while leaving the student’s on-policy rollout unchanged. Second, we develop Multi-Solution Dual-Level GRPO, which combines action-level supervision with history-conditioned, per-state planning-quality supervision while accounting for multiple valid actions at each logged GUI state. Together, these stages support multi-step GUI tasks without requiring the student to reproduce fixed demonstration trajectories. We further develop a scalable data generation pipeline and a corresponding multi-solution dataset, Lite-Dataset, to support the training and evaluation of GUI agents, addressing a gap in the existing literature. Extensive experiments across multiple GUI benchmarks demonstrate that LiteGUI substantially improves the performance of lightweight GUI agents over existing training paradigms, including SFT, on-policy distillation and GRPO, and achieves competitive or superior performance compared with substantially larger models.

1 Introduction

Automated computer use has received increasing attention in recent years (Hurst et al., 2024; Parker Lyman, 2025; anthropic, 2026; Team et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2025a). Among these approaches, GUI agents represent a specialized class of systems that leverage visual understanding to interpret and execute computer-based tasks. While prior work has primarily focused on building GUI agents using large-scale models (Qin et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a; Agashe et al., 2025), the development of lightweight models 11 1 By a lightweight model, we refer to models in the 2-3B parameter range. for efficient deployment is challenging and remains largely underexplored. Smaller models are typically considered insufficient for handling such complex tasks due to their limited capacity. We observe that the commonly used supervised fine-tuning (SFT) paradigm—particularly for smaller models—tends to overfit to domain-specific and fixed interaction trajectories. This limitation degrades zero-shot generalization and hinders effective error recovery in dynamic UI environments. In this paper, we propose a new approach, named LiteGUI, to improve the performance of lightweight GUI agents through on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning.

While distillation has been successfully applied to tasks such as summarization, translation, and arithmetic reasoning (e.g., GKD (Agarwal et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Shenfeld et al., 2026)), its effectiveness in GUI agent settings remains limited. This is largely due to the higher task complexity and the relatively weaker performance of available teacher models. To address the challenges, we propose Guided On-Policy Distillation (Guided-OPD), to ensure that the teacher model provides reliable guidance by conditioning on training-time privileged information derived from human-verified valid-action annotations. Furthermore, to account for the multi-solution nature of GUI tasks, the proposed method compares the student’s on-policy output with the valid-action set for the current GUI state and selects the most-matched valid action, providing adaptive action-level guidance without imposing a single fixed target completion at each logged state.

In addition, careful design of reinforcement learning (RL) strategies is essential to address the challenges inherent in GUI-based tasks. Existing RL approaches are often limited by their reliance on single-solution rewards, lack of long-horizon planning, and susceptibility to losing state context during execution. To overcome these limitations, we propose a Multi-Solution Dual-Level GRPO. First the method includes dual-level reward framework that jointly supports long-term planning and short-term execution. At the macro level, we introduce robust, model-evaluated subtask rewards that provide structured guidance for decomposing complex, long-horizon tasks. At the micro level, by integrating real-time state perception and trajectory recording, the framework dynamically aligns low-level execution outcomes with an equivalent multi-solution set, thereby mitigating the “false negative” penalties induced by rigid single-label supervision, and thus improving the execution precision while robustly preserving generalization across diverse and complex UI scenarios. In summary, the core contributions of this paper are:

We propose LiteGUI, a novel framework for building lightweight GUI agents that addresses the unique challenges of GUI interaction tasks, including the long-horizon nature of complex tasks, the existence of multiple valid interaction paths, and the limited availability of capable models and high-quality training data. Specifically, we propose (1) Most-Matched Guided On-Policy Distillation, which selects the valid action most closely aligned with the student’s current output from the human-verified valid-action set, using it only as training-time privileged teacher guidance to reduce hallucinations and supervision–state mismatch; and (2) Multi-Solution Dual-Level GRPO, which integrates robust model-evaluated subtask-planning rewards with multi-solution action-set matching to jointly support long-horizon planning and short-horizon perception and execution. Notably, LiteGUI is SFT-free, avoiding the need for supervised fine-tuning on static trajectories and thereby mitigating catastrophic forgetting of foundational capabilities and policy overfitting in small-scale models;

Evaluations on ScreenSpot-Pro (Li et al., 2025), OS-World (Xie et al., 2024), and Lite-Bench demonstrate that our approach enables lightweight models to achieve substantial gains in GUI task success rates. Our LiteGUI model achieves strong performance among lightweight models, over existing training paradigms, including SFT, on-policy distillation and GRPO, and becomes competitive with much larger-scale models on the reported comparisons;

Finally, to support the training and evaluation of the distillation and RL exploration paradigms, we design an automated data generation pipeline and curate Lite-Dataset, comprising 30K GUI trajectories and 11K multi-solution annotations. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first available multi-solution GUI agent dataset. Besides, we also introduce Lite-Bench, a 160-task benchmark covering File System, Web, and Terminal. All resources will be publicly released for community.

2 Related Work

2.1 Vision-based GUI Agents

Early GUI agents predominantly relied on underlying system APIs or accessibility trees, which severely hindered their cross-platform generalization (Deng et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2024). Recently, the research paradigm has rapidly shifted toward vision-only agents, primarily bifurcating into two approaches: the direct application of powerful general-purpose Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) (e.g., GPT-4o(Hurst et al., 2024), Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Qwen-VL(Bai et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2025a)), and the fine-tuning of domain-specific GUI vision models (e.g., CogAgent (Hong et al., 2024), UI-TARS (Qin et al., 2025), OpenCUA (Wang et al., 2025) and others (Lin et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2025)) utilizing large-scale interaction data (Gou et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025). While these models exhibit exceptional planning and execution performance in the GUI domain, their formidable capabilities incur prohibitive computational overhead during inference, severely impeding practical deployment and user experience. Consequently, developing lightweight agents (e.g., 2B/A3B-scale models) has become an urgent imperative to address these bottlenecks. However, the post-training of current lightweight models relies almost exclusively on traditional Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) (Hsieh et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025) or Reinforcement Learning (RL) (Shen et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025) methods utilizing naive coordinate rewards (e.g., GRPO). This coarse-grained training paradigm is precisely the root cause of the policy rigidity and capability degradation observed in small-scale models during long-horizon, multi-step exploration.

2.2 Post-training for GUI Agents

To improve the interaction capabilities of GUI agents, post-training paradigms are shifting from static imitation toward dynamic exploration. However, most existing approaches still rely on SFT over static trajectories, which suffers from covariate shift in multi-step decision-making (Ross et al., 2011), leading to rapid error accumulation once deviating from expert paths. Moreover, fitting long sequential data can disrupt the visual representation capabilities of lightweight models, resulting in catastrophic forgetting (Zeng et al., 2024). To address these limitations, recent work explores policy distillation methods (e.g., GKD (Agarwal et al., 2024), SDFT (Shenfeld et al., 2026), and others (Chen et al., 2025)), where teacher models provide real-time guidance during student exploration. However, such approaches remain underexplored in GUI agents, primarily due to the susceptibility of large models to hallucinations in “closed-book” settings (Alansari & Luqman, 2026; Huang et al., 2025), which introduce noisy supervision and degrade multi-step trajectory execution. We therefore propose Guided On-Policy Distillation to leverage human-verified valid-action annotations to mitigate hallucinations and employ most-matched valid-action selection to accommodate the multi-solution nature of GUI tasks, enabling flexible action-level exploration. Furthermore, reinforcement learning (RL) methods (e.g., GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) and SAPO (Gao et al., 2025)) have been applied to vision-based models (e.g., VLM-R1 (Shen et al., 2025)). However, existing reward designs based on exact coordinate/action matching (Lu et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025) suffer from sparsity and false negatives, limiting generalization. To address this, we introduce a multi-solution dual-level RL mechanism: macro-level subtask rewards evaluated by strong models, and micro-level dynamic matching over multi-solution actions, improving optimization in long-horizon exploration.

3 Method

We propose a two-stage training paradigm for GUI agents, shown in Fig.1. In the first stage, we introduce Guided-OPD, which leverages multi-solution action annotations as training-time privileged information to provide a more stable supervisory signal for distillation. In the second stage, we introduce Multi-Solution Dual-Level GRPO (MD-GRPO), which improves reinforcement learning by incorporating a multi-solution reward for action correctness and a history-conditioned, per-state reward for evaluating subtask-plan quality. To achieve this two-stage training paradigm, both distillation and reinforcement learning datasets are required, especially those with multi-solution annotations. We develop a data generation pipeline to semi-automatically produce multi-solution GUI task trajectories for training. Details of the pipeline are illustrated in Fig. 1. In the following subsections, we first introduce the task formulation of the GUI agent, followed by the details of Guided-OPD and MD-GRPO.

3.1 Task Formulation

Given a user instruction qq (e.g., lower the computer volume), the GUI model input xtx_{t} is denoted as:

xt(w)=(q,st−w,yt−w,…,st−1,yt−1,st),x_{t}^{(w)}=\left(q,s_{t-w},y_{t-w},\dots,s_{t-1},y_{t-1},s_{t}\right), (1)

where sts_{t} denotes the GUI screenshot at time step tt, yty_{t} denotes the structured model output. ww is the observation window size, i.e., the input consists of the user instruction, the current state, and the previous states and outputs within a history window of size ww. The model output yty_{t} contains three key components:

yt={rt,ct,at},y_{t}=\{r_{t},c_{t},a_{t}\}, (2)

where rtr_{t} denotes the Reasoning field, ctc_{t} denotes the subtask list, and ata_{t} denotes the executable GUI action (e.g., the mouse and keyboard actions). The Reasoning field follows an Observation–Intent–Analysis structure. For example, it may describe the current UI observation, infer that the user intends to open a website, and conclude that the next step should be clicking the address bar. The subtask field serves as an explicit planning and memory state for the agent, provides a compact mechanism for carrying long-horizon task state across steps. For example, it may contain items such as “enter the target URL”, “log into the account”, and “check whether the homepage has loaded”. These entries store task-level information that may not be fully recoverable from the latest screenshot alone, including subtask completion status, key intermediate milestones, and visual clues extracted from previous observations. Thus, the recent screenshots provide local perceptual context, while subtasks preserve higher-level progress information. We represent the executable action as

at=(τt,pt,vt),a_{t}=(\tau_{t},p_{t},v_{t}), (3)

where τt\tau_{t} is the action type, ptp_{t} is the position argument, and vtv_{t} is the text or key-value argument. For example, a click action can be represented as τt=CLICK\tau_{t}=\texttt{CLICK} with pt=(521,41)p_{t}=(521,41), while a text-input action can be represented as τt=TEXT_INPUT\tau_{t}=\texttt{TEXT\_INPUT} with vt=www.example.comv_{t}=\texttt{www.example.com}. The model predicts a point pt=(x,y)p_{t}=(x,y); for grounding supervision, the corresponding human annotation may specify a target bounding box b∗=[xmin,ymin,xmax,ymax]b^{*}=[x_{\min},y_{\min},x_{\max},y_{\max}].

For each state xtx_{t}, we maintain a set of human-verified valid actions as ground truths:

𝒜t∗={at∗(1),at∗(2),…,at∗(K)},\mathcal{A}^{*}_{t}=\{a^{*(1)}_{t},a^{*(2)}_{t},\dots,a^{*(K)}_{t}\}, (4)

which contains KK multiple actions that can correctly advance the task from the current GUI state. It should be viewed as a finite approximation of the valid action space rather than an exhaustive set of all possible correct actions.

3.2 Guided On-Policy Distillation

In standard Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD) or On-Policy Distillation (OPD), the student first samples an output a^t\hat{a}_{t} conditioned on the current input xtx_{t}, and the teacher evaluates the sampled sequence under teacher forcing. This evaluation produces full next-token distributions at all valid completion prefixes. However, in GUI agent training, student outputs are often noisy: they may contain incorrect action types, inaccurate coordinates, wrong text arguments, or invalid JSON structures. If the teacher evaluates such outputs using only the default context, the resulting likelihood signal can be unstable. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a Guided-OPD mechanism, which provides the teacher with additional action guidance constructed from the human-verified valid action set 𝒜t∗\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*}, We denote this teacher-side guidance as:

gt=h⁡(𝒜t∗,a^t),g_{t}=h(\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*},\hat{a}_{t}), (5)

where h⁡(⋅)h(\cdot) specifies how the annotated valid actions are converted into the teacher-side action guidance. In this way, the teacher distribution is conditioned on πT(⋅∣xt,gt)\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x_{t},g_{t}), whereas the student policy remains πθ(⋅∣xt)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{t}). Note that the guidance gtg_{t} is derived only from the current-step human-verified valid action set 𝒜t∗\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*} and is used exclusively on the teacher side during training. It is never provided to the student model and is not used at inference time. Therefore, this framework can be viewed as a form of training-time privileged guidance, following the learning-using-privileged-information paradigm (Vapnik & Vashist, 2009; Vapnik & Izmailov, 2015), and as a privileged-information extension of on-policy distillation (Lopez-Paz et al., 2015; Agarwal et al., 2024). Different guidance variants h⁡(⋅)h(\cdot) correspond to different ways of mapping 𝒜t∗\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*} into gtg_{t}. We consider three variants: Single-GT, Multi-GT and Most-Matched-GT Guided-OPD in this paper.

(1) Single-GT Guided-OPD. One valid action is randomly sampled from 𝒜t∗\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*} and provided to the teacher as the reference action:

gt=at∗(k),k∼Uniform⁡{1,…,K}.g_{t}=a_{t}^{*(k)},\quad k\sim\mathrm{Uniform}\{1,\dots,K\}. (6)

This gives the teacher additional task constraints, but the randomly selected ground truth may be far from the student’s current output, leading to a mismatch between the selected reference action and the student’s current output.

(2) Multi-GT Guided-OPD. The full valid action set is provided to the teacher:

gt=𝒜t∗.g_{t}=\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*}. (7)

This exposes the teacher to all annotated valid actions for the current state. However, it may also increase the complexity of the teacher context and lead to a more diffuse likelihood estimate across multiple possible actions.

(3) Most-Matched-GT Guided-OPD. Given the student-generated output y^t\hat{y}_{t}, we select the valid action that is most matched to the student’s current on-policy behavior:

gt=at†=arg⁡maxa∗∈𝒜t∗​ϕgui​(y^t,a∗),g_{t}=a_{t}^{\dagger}=\arg\max_{a^{*}\in\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*}}\phi_{\mathrm{gui}}(\hat{y}_{t},a^{*}), (8)

where ϕgui\phi_{\mathrm{gui}} is the unified GUI action matching function defined as:

ϕgui​(y^t,a∗)=wτmτ+𝕀[b∗≠∅]wpmp+𝕀[v∗≠∅]wvmvwτ+𝕀[b∗≠∅]wp+𝕀[v∗≠∅]wv.\phi_{\mathrm{gui}}(\hat{y}_{t},a^{*})=\frac{w_{\tau}m_{\tau}+\mathbb{I}[b^{*}\neq\emptyset]w_{p}m_{p}+\mathbb{I}[v^{*}\neq\emptyset]w_{v}m_{v}}{w_{\tau}+\mathbb{I}[b^{*}\neq\emptyset]w_{p}+\mathbb{I}[v^{*}\neq\emptyset]w_{v}}. (9)

mτ=𝕀[τ^t=τ∗]m_{\tau}=\mathbb{I}[\hat{\tau}_{t}=\tau^{*}] measures action-type correctness, mp∈[0,1]m_{p}\in[0,1] measures the alignment between the predicted position p^t\hat{p}_{t} and the target bounding box b∗b^{*}, and mv∈[0,1]m_{v}\in[0,1] measures exact or partial matching between the predicted value v^t\hat{v}_{t} and the annotated value v∗v^{*}. The indicator terms ensure that position and value scores are only considered when the corresponding annotations are available. Details of mτm_{\tau}, mpm_{p}, mvm_{v}, and corresponding coefficients wτw_{\tau}, wpw_{p}, wvw_{v} are provided in Appendix A.2. If the student output cannot be parsed into a valid GUI action, all candidate actions receive zero matching scores, and we fall back to a deterministic reference action from 𝒜t∗\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*}. This selection mechanism provides the teacher with a reference action that is aligned with the student’s current on-policy output. Compared with Single-GT, it reduces the mismatch caused by random or fixed reference selection. Compared with Multi-GT, it provides a more focused reference signal while avoiding an overly complex teacher context.

Full-vocabulary reverse-KL OPD. After obtaining gtg_{t}, we construct the input of teacher model as

x~t=[q,st−w,yt−w,…,st−1,yt−1,st,reference_action=gt].\tilde{x}_{t}=[q,s_{t-w},y_{t-w},\dots,s_{t-1},y_{t-1},s_{t},\texttt{reference\_action}=g_{t}]. (10)

The student samples a completion y^t∼πθ(⋅∣xt)\hat{y}_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{t}). The sampled token sequence and the discrete teacher-side guidance gtg_{t} are treated as fixed during the optimization step. Let ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t} denote the non-masked completion positions. At each valid position j∈ℳtj\in\mathcal{M}_{t}, we compute the full-vocabulary student and teacher distributions:

pθ,j=πθ(⋅∣xt,y^t,<j),pT,jgt=πT(⋅∣x~t,y^t,<j).p_{\theta,j}=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{t},\hat{y}_{t,<j}),\qquad p_{T,j}^{g_{t}}=\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid\tilde{x}_{t},\hat{y}_{t,<j}). (11)

Following GKD (Agarwal et al., 2024), the objective is the full-vocabulary, per-prefix divergence:

ℒOPD=1|ℳt|​∑j∈ℳtDβ​(pθ,j∥sg⁡[pT,jgt]),β=1,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}_{t}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{M}_{t}}D_{\beta}\left(p_{\theta,j}\,\middle\|\,\operatorname{sg}\left[p_{T,j}^{g_{t}}\right]\right),\qquad\beta=1, (12)

where sg⁡[⋅]\operatorname{sg}[\cdot] denotes stop-gradient (identity in the forward pass, with zero gradient), and DβD_{\beta} denotes the generalized JSD/KL family used by our implementation. Under our parameterization, β=1\beta=1 selects reverse KL:

D1(p∥q)=DKL(p∥q)=∑vp(v)logp⁡(v)q⁡(v).D_{1}(p\|q)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=\sum_{v}p(v)\log\frac{p(v)}{q(v)}. (13)

The loss is computed over the full vocabulary, rather than only the sampled token, with gradients flowing only through the student distribution. See Appendix A.5 for implementation details.

3.3 Multi-Solution Dual-Level GRPO

We further optimize the student using GRPO. Unlike standard single-answer tasks, GUI control exhibits strong multi-solution equivalence: under the same GUI state, multiple actions may validly advance the task. For example, a file can be opened by double-clicking it or by selecting it and pressing Enter; a web page can be reached by clicking a shortcut or directly typing the URL. Therefore, a reward based on a single ground-truth action may incorrectly penalize valid alternative actions.

We focus on two reward-design questions that are central to GUI agent training: how to avoid false negatives caused by single-reference supervision, and how to evaluate whether the model understands the current task stage and can re-plan when necessary. We address these questions using the multi-solution action reward and planning reward. For each logged input xtx_{t}, the behavior policy samples GG candidate outputs:

{y^t(1),y^t(2),…,y^t(G)}∼πθold(⋅∣xt).\{\hat{y}_{t}^{(1)},\hat{y}_{t}^{(2)},\dots,\hat{y}_{t}^{(G)}\}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(\cdot\mid x_{t}). (14)

Training uses logged GUI states rather than live environment rollouts: all candidates are scored at the same state using the trajectory context and human-verified annotations. The total reward for the ii-th candidate is

Rt(i)=λm​s​Rms​(y^t(i),𝒜t∗)+λs​u​b​Rsub​(y^t(i))+λf​o​r​m​a​t/l​e​n​g​t​h​Rformat/length​(y^t(i)),R_{t}^{(i)}=\lambda_{ms}R_{\mathrm{ms}}(\hat{y}_{t}^{(i)},\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*})+\lambda_{sub}R_{\mathrm{sub}}(\hat{y}_{t}^{(i)})+\lambda_{format/length}R_{\mathrm{format/length}}(\hat{y}_{t}^{(i)}), (15)

where RmsR_{\mathrm{ms}} is the multi-solution GUI action reward, RsubR_{\mathrm{sub}} is the planning reward, and Rformat/lengthR_{\mathrm{format/length}} is the JSON-aware soft overlength reward. λm​s\lambda_{ms}, λs​u​b\lambda_{sub} and λf​o​r​m​a​t/l​e​n​g​t​h\lambda_{format/length} are the coefficients for each reward term. Detailed hyperparameter settings can be found in Appendix A.6.

Multi-Solution Action Reward. Given the multi-solution action set 𝒜t∗\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*}, we compare the model output against all valid candidate actions and take the maximum score as:

Rms​(y^t,𝒜t∗)=maxa∗∈𝒜t∗⁡ϕgui​(y^t,a∗).R_{\mathrm{ms}}(\hat{y}_{t},\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*})=\max_{a^{*}\in\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*}}\phi_{\mathrm{gui}}(\hat{y}_{t},a^{*}). (16)

where ϕgui\phi_{\mathrm{gui}} is the unified GUI action matching function defined in Eq. 9. This changes the reward criterion from “does the model reproduce this specific annotated action?” to “does the model match any acceptable action?” Since a single annotation is usually only one sample from the space of valid GUI actions, max-over-solutions substantially reduces false negative rewards caused by fixed annotation paths. From an optimization perspective, single-ground-truth rewards can incorrectly convert differences among equivalent action paths into negative feedback, discouraging exploration of valid alternatives. In contrast, the multi-solution reward gives positive feedback when the model output matches any annotated acceptable action for the current logged state.

Planning Reward for Long-Horizon Tasks. The multi-solution action reward provides action-level supervision by matching each candidate output against annotated acceptable actions for the current logged GUI state. For multi-step GUI tasks, a complementary planning signal can assess whether a proposed subtask plan reflects task progress and the intended next step. We therefore introduce a history-conditioned, per-state planning-quality reward for this purpose. The reward scores the current candidate subtask plan ctc_{t}, which compactly represents task progress, using the available trajectory context. It therefore evaluates intermediate plan quality at the current logged state rather than the outcome of executing a candidate action. The frozen VLM judge uses the task, available screenshot history, and previous model outputs as context and returns a score:

Rsub=fjudge(q,st−w:t,yt−w:t−1,ct),Rsub∈[0,1].R_{\mathrm{sub}}=f_{\mathrm{judge}}(q,s_{t-w:t},y_{t-w:t-1},c_{t}),\quad R_{\mathrm{sub}}\in[0,1]. (17)

It evaluates the plan along four dimensions: task relevance and adaptability, visual grounding, decomposition granularity, and state consistency. In particular, when the latest screenshot indicates that the agent is stuck, in an error state, or in a loop, the judge is instructed to assign a low score unless the subtask plan explicitly reflects the abnormal state and proposes a corrective next step. Together, the two rewards provide action-level supervision and history-conditioned plan-quality supervision.

GRPO Objective. For the GG candidate outputs sampled from the same input, we normalize rewards within the group to obtain the relative advantage:

A^t(i)=Rt(i)−mean⁡({Rt(j)}j=1G)std⁡({Rt(j)}j=1G)+ϵadv.\hat{A}^{(i)}_{t}=\frac{R^{(i)}_{t}-\mathrm{mean}(\{R^{(j)}_{t}\}_{j=1}^{G})}{\mathrm{std}(\{R^{(j)}_{t}\}_{j=1}^{G})+\epsilon_{\mathrm{adv}}}. (18)

Here ϵadv\epsilon_{\mathrm{adv}} is the numerical stabilizer for reward normalization and is distinct from the clipping bounds ϵlow\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}} and ϵhigh\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}. We then optimize the policy using the GRPO clipped objective:

ℒGRPO=−1G∑i=1Gmin(ρt(i)A^t(i),clip(ρt(i),1−ϵlow,1+ϵhigh)A^t(i))+βKLDKL(πθ∥πref),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}=-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\min\left(\rho^{(i)}_{t}\hat{A}^{(i)}_{t},\mathrm{clip}\left(\rho^{(i)}_{t},1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}},1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}\right)\hat{A}^{(i)}_{t}\right)+\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}), (19)

where the sequence-level policy ratio is computed from the mean token log-probability difference:

ρt(i)=exp⁡[1|ℳt(i)|​∑j∈ℳt(i)(log⁡πθ​(y^t,j(i)∣xt,y^t,<j(i))−log⁡πθold​(y^t,j(i)∣xt,y^t,<j(i)))].\rho^{(i)}_{t}=\exp\!\left[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}^{(i)}_{t}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{M}^{(i)}_{t}}\left(\log\pi_{\theta}(\hat{y}^{(i)}_{t,j}\mid x_{t},\hat{y}^{(i)}_{t,<j})-\log\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(\hat{y}^{(i)}_{t,j}\mid x_{t},\hat{y}^{(i)}_{t,<j})\right)\right]. (20)

Here, ℳt(i)\mathcal{M}^{(i)}_{t} denotes the valid completion-token positions, πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}} is the behavior policy used to sample candidates, and πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is the reference model. Detailed hyperparameter settings are in Appendix A.6.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

We implement Lite-GUI using two representative backbones: Qwen3-VL-2B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B, and employ Qwen3-VL-32B as the teacher model. To implement Lite-GUI, a multi-solution dataset is required. However, no such dataset is currently available in the community. We therefore develop an automated data pipeline (illustrated in Figure 1), to construct Lite-Dataset, which contains 11K multi-solution samples. More details about the data construction pipeline and Lite-Dataset are provided in the Appendix A.7 and A.8. In MD-GRPO, we use Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct as the sub-task planning judge because it is community-friendly while can still provide strong alignment with human judgments, achieving 90.0% human agreement from our study. Its prompt, calibration metrics, and limitations are provided in Appendix A.4. All models are trained on a cluster of NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Details on hyper-parameters are provided in Appendix A.5 and A.6.

We evaluate Lite-GUI on ScreenSpot-Pro (Li et al., 2025) and OS-World (Xie et al., 2024), two of the most widely used benchmarks for GUI agents, alongside Lite-Bench, our newly curated benchmark. Lite-Bench comprises 160 tasks (up to 18 steps), featuring 75 web tasks, 38 terminal tasks, and 47 file system tasks that strictly prohibit terminal usage to enforce pure vision-based interaction. It is worth noting that Lite-Bench is in a similar domain to Lite-Dataset, but with no overlapping data. Details of Lite-Bench can be referred to Appendix A.9. Each reported result for our models and ablations is the arithmetic mean over five independent runs. Below, we first compare Lite-GUI with widely used training paradigms and then compare our models with state-of-the-art (SOTA) models.

4.2 Effectiveness of LiteGUI

We first compare Lite-GUI with widely used training paradigms for GUI agents, including SFT, GRPO, and OPD, as well as ablations of individual components of Lite-GUI, across all three benchmarks in Table 1. To ensure a fair comparison, all training methods use the same Qwen3-VL-2B backbone and the same Lite-Dataset. The reported results are averaged over five independent runs. We observe that SFT actually degrades performance on both ScreenSpot-Pro and OS-World, potentially due to overfitting and catastrophic forgetting in the lightweight GUI-agent setting. In contrast, Lite-GUI (last row) achieves the best performance across all three benchmarks.

A closer examination of the ablations shows that Guided-OPD outperforms vanilla OPD, while Most-Matched Guided-OPD achieves the best, demonstrating the benefit of using the guided supervision. Moreover, incorporating either multi-solution or dual-level rewards in GRPO further improves performance, while combining all components achieves the strongest overall results. Notably, OS-World and Lite-Bench contain more complex, long-horizon GUI agent tasks, whereas ScreenSpot-Pro focuses primarily on visual grounding and single-step interaction. Consequently, Lite-GUI yields larger gains on OS-World and Lite-Bench, highlighting the effectiveness of guided planning and multi-solution learning for complex, long-horizon GUI interaction.

We further conduct a detailed analysis of Guided-OPD. Across 50 multi-solution validation states, privileged guidance improves the teacher’s discrimination between valid and invalid GUI actions, increasing pairwise preference accuracy from 46% to 77% and yielding a cleaner supervision signal for OPD. Guided-OPD also improves the validity and diversity of the student’s generated actions without causing policy collapse toward a narrow subset of valid solutions. Overall, Most-Matched-GT strengthens both teacher supervision and student action generation while preserving coverage of multiple valid interaction paths. Further details are provided in Appendix A.10.

4.3 Comparison with SOTA Methods

We then compare our Lite-GUI models with state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches on ScreenSpot-Pro, OS-World, and Lite-Bench in Tables 2, 3, and 4, respectively. We train both Qwen3-VL-2B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B using Lite-GUI. For ScreenSpot-Pro, we build upon the widely used ShowUI-Desktop-8K (Lin et al., 2024) dataset, which is publicly available for this task. We augment it with multi-solution annotations generated using our data pipeline, rather than using our Lite-Dataset. For OS-World and Lite-Bench, no publicly available training datasets are provided for these benchmarks. Therefore, we use our Lite-Dataset to train the models on both benchmarks.

As shown in Table 2, On ScreenSpot-Pro, Lite-GUI-2B achieves an average accuracy of 46.86%, setting a new SOTA among models of the same parameter scale. Notably, it also surpasses significantly larger specialized models, including UI-TARS-72B (38.1%). Remarkably, while existing methods typically rely on extensive training data, Lite-GUI-2B attains these strong results using only the 8K-sample ShowUI-Desktop-8K dataset. This high data efficiency highlights the effectiveness of our LiteGUI framework in GUI reasoning. Furthermore, Lite-GUI-30B-A3B achieves SOTA performance (58.95%) across all compared models, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.

From Table 3, Lite-GUI-2B achieves a 13.24% success rate on OSWorld, more than doubling the performance of its backbone Qwen3-VL-2B (6.04%). Lite-GUI-30B-A3B further pushes the performance to 22.7%, achieving the best performance among models of the same parameter scale while rivaling top-tier specialized models with substantially larger parameters (72B). It is also worth noting that, without training on large-scale datasets as in OpenCUA and UI-TARS, our Lite-GUI model can still achieve comparable results, demonstrating the data efficiency of our method. On Lite-Bench (Table 4), Lite-GUI-2B achieves a 63.13% success rate, representing nearly a 2×\times improvement over the vanilla baseline (32.35%). These substantial gains validate the effectiveness of our approach, with similar trends observed for Lite-GUI-30B-A3B, which achieves a success rate of up to 88.75%.

5 Conclusion

We have proposed Lite-GUI, a new training paradigm for building lightweight GUI agents. Lite-GUI leverages multi-solution guided distillation and dual-level GRPO to address the unique challenges of GUI tasks, which are often complex, long-horizon, and inherently multi-path, while also facing a lack of strong teacher models at comparable scales. Our approach achieves substantial improvements over existing baselines, reaching SOTA performance among models at comparable scales and delivering competitive results with significantly larger models across all benchmarks. We have also developed a scalable, automated pipeline for generating multi-solution GUI data, resulting in the 11K-sample Lite-Dataset, which is currently lacking in the community. Future work will explore incorporating online interaction with real-world environments to further improve agent performance, as well as further scaling down the model size to enable more practical on-device deployment.

AI use statement

In this work, we used generative AI tools for the following tasks that require disclosure: generating synthetic GUI interaction data using the pipeline in Appendix A.7, assisting with translation of manuscript text, and assisting with the implementation of methods and with the creation or editing of code. We have not used generative AI tools to develop theoretical models or conceptual frameworks, to formulate or prove mathematical claims, to propose or refine hypotheses, to design or provide feedback on research methodology or experiments, to clean or reformat datasets, to support qualitative or thematic data analysis, or to interpret results; these tasks are therefore not applicable to this work. Additionally, we used generative AI tools for a task with recommended disclosure, namely drafting and editing manuscript sections for readability. All AI-assisted outputs were reviewed by the authors: AI-assisted code was tested for correctness, and AI-assisted text was checked against the cited literature and our experimental results. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

Ethics statement

This work studies GUI agents that control a computer from screenshots. Such systems can improve productivity and accessibility, but they can also perform unintended operations, leak information visible on screen, or be misused for unauthorized automation. Our training data consist of GUI screenshots and synthetic interaction trajectories; we remove sensitive content during data construction and release only assets that we are permitted to distribute. Practical deployment should include permission control, confirmation of sensitive actions, execution logging, and privacy filtering. Our experiments involve no human subjects. A detailed discussion of limitations, broader impacts, and asset licenses is provided in Appendix A.12 and Appendix A.13.

Reproducibility statement

We describe the task formulation and the two training stages in Section 3, and the benchmark setup and evaluation protocols in Section 4. Implementation details, hyperparameters, the judge prompt, and the data pipeline are given in Appendix A.5, Appendix A.6, Appendix A.4, and Appendix A.7. We will publicly release the Lite-Dataset, Lite-Bench, and the training and evaluation code to support reproduction.

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Ground-truth Guidance Variants

Let 𝒜t∗\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*} denote the human-verified valid action set for the current GUI state. The teacher-side guidance gtg_{t} is constructed from 𝒜t∗\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*}.

For Single-GT Guided-OPD, one valid action is randomly sampled:

gt=at∗(k),k∼Uniform⁡{1,…,K}.g_{t}=a_{t}^{*(k)},\quad k\sim\mathrm{Uniform}\{1,\dots,K\}. (21)

For Multi-GT Guided-OPD, the full valid action set is provided:

gt=𝒜t∗.g_{t}=\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*}. (22)

For Guided-OPD, the guidance is selected according to:

gt=at†=arg⁡maxa∗∈𝒜t∗⁡S⁡(a^t,a∗).g_{t}=a_{t}^{\dagger}=\arg\max_{a^{*}\in\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*}}S(\hat{a}_{t},a^{*}). (23)

All three variants use the same student input xtx_{t} and differ only in the privileged teacher context.

A.2 Action Matching and Multi-Solution Reward Details

We define the base GUI action matcher ϕgui​(y^t,a∗)\phi_{\mathrm{gui}}(\hat{y}_{t},a^{*}) as a normalized score in [0,1][0,1]. If the model output cannot be parsed as a valid JSON action or violates the required action schema, the score is set to zero. For the reported runs, the component weights are wτ=10w_{\tau}=10, wp=5w_{p}=5, and wv=4w_{v}=4; with the value-matching scores below, an exact value match contributes 4 and a partial match contributes 2 before normalization.

Action type matching.
mτ=𝕀[τ^=τ∗].m_{\tau}=\mathbb{I}[\hat{\tau}=\tau^{*}]. (24)
Position matching.

For position-based actions, the model predicts a point p^\hat{p} and the annotation provides a target bounding box b∗b^{*}. We use a continuous position score mp∈[0,1]m_{p}\in[0,1]. If the predicted point falls inside the central region of the target box, mp=1m_{p}=1. If it falls inside the full box but outside the central region, the score is linearly interpolated between 0.50.5 and 11. If it falls outside the box, the score decays exponentially with the distance dd to the box boundary:

mp=0.5exp(−d/200).m_{p}=0.5\exp(-d/200). (25)
Value matching.

For text or key-value actions, we compute:

mv={1,exact match,0.5,partial match,0,otherwise.m_{v}=\begin{cases}1,&\text{exact match},\\ 0.5,&\text{partial match},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (26)
Combined score.

The final action matching score is:

ϕgui​(y^t,a∗)=wτmτ+𝕀[b∗≠∅]wpmp+𝕀[v∗≠∅]wvmvwτ+𝕀[b∗≠∅]wp+𝕀[v∗≠∅]wv.\phi_{\mathrm{gui}}(\hat{y}_{t},a^{*})=\frac{w_{\tau}m_{\tau}+\mathbb{I}[b^{*}\neq\emptyset]w_{p}m_{p}+\mathbb{I}[v^{*}\neq\emptyset]w_{v}m_{v}}{w_{\tau}+\mathbb{I}[b^{*}\neq\emptyset]w_{p}+\mathbb{I}[v^{*}\neq\emptyset]w_{v}}. (27)

Given multiple valid actions, we use:

Rms​(y^t,𝒜t∗)=maxa∗∈𝒜t∗⁡ϕgui​(y^t,a∗).R_{\mathrm{ms}}(\hat{y}_{t},\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*})=\max_{a^{*}\in\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*}}\phi_{\mathrm{gui}}(\hat{y}_{t},a^{*}). (28)

A.3 Planning Reward Details

The planning reward is a history-conditioned, per-state plan-quality signal computed for candidate subtask plans at logged GUI states using an external VLM judge. The judge receives the user instruction, available screenshot history, previous model outputs, and the current candidate subtask plan. Candidate actions are not executed for reward computation, and the reward uses neither sampled future states nor terminal task-success feedback; it is therefore a local surrogate for plan quality, not an estimate of long-term return or verified task recovery.

The judge evaluates the plan along four dimensions:

  1. 1.

    Task relevance and adaptability: whether the plan reflects the user instruction and adapts to the current UI state.

  2. 2.

    Visual grounding: whether the plan is grounded in actual UI elements visible in the screenshots.

  3. 3.

    Decomposition granularity: whether the plan decomposes the task into actionable subtasks at an appropriate granularity.

  4. 4.

    State consistency: whether the completion status of subtasks is consistent with the latest screenshot.

If the latest screenshot indicates that the agent is stuck, in an error state, or in a loop, the first unfinished subtask must explicitly propose a corrective next step. If the plan ignores the obstacle, remains overly high-level, or contains completion markers inconsistent with the latest screenshot, the judge is instructed to assign a score below 0.50.5.

The judge is required to return a structured JSON score:

{"score": 0.8}

A.4 Training-time Planning Judge: Prompt and Reliability

We use a frozen Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct model as the VLM judge for the planning reward. The judge is queried only during RL training. The temperature is set to 00, and the judge is instructed to output a structured JSON score from the discrete set {0.0,0.3,0.5,0.8,1.0}\{0.0,0.3,0.5,0.8,1.0\}. For detailed prompt design, please refer to Fig.  2.

Human–judge agreement.

On a held-out calibration subset, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct achieves 90.0% exact agreement with human annotations (Cohen’s κ=0.7916\kappa=0.7916). Treating high-quality trajectories as the positive class gives 94.52% recall, 81.18% precision, and 87.34% F1. These metrics assess the training-time planning reward judge, not the GPT-5.4 evaluator used to judge Lite-Bench task success (Appendix A.9).

Scope and limitations.

The lower precision suggests an optimistic bias; this offline agreement study does not rule out reward hacking during training. The reward coefficients are 0.30 for planning, 0.60 for action matching, and 0.10 for format/length; these are weights, not fixed shares of realized reward.

A.5 Generalized Knowledge Distillation

We first optimize the policy with generalized knowledge distillation (GKD). The teacher is Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, and the students are Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B. All GKD runs use full-parameter bfloat16 training with the Megatron backend. Unlike offline distillation from fixed target responses, our GKD stage is on-policy: the student generates the completion that is used for distillation. Concretely, we set the GKD on-policy probability to λ=1.0\lambda=1.0, enable vLLM rollout, and disable sequential teacher generation. The dataset therefore provides prompts and human-verified valid-action candidates for constructing the privileged guidance described in the main text, while the optimized response tokens are sampled from the current student policy.

For each GUI state xtx_{t}, the student samples a completion y^t∼πθ(⋅∣xt)\hat{y}_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{t}). The sampled completion is held fixed during the optimization step. The teacher and student are each evaluated once on the full sampled completion sequence under teacher forcing. In Guided-OPD, the teacher receives the most-matched valid action gtg_{t} from Section 3.2 as privileged guidance, and its input is x~t=[xt,reference_action=gt]\tilde{x}_{t}=[x_{t},\texttt{reference\_action}=g_{t}]. The discrete teacher-side guidance gtg_{t} is also held fixed during the optimization step. Let ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t} denote the non-masked completion positions in y^t\hat{y}_{t}. This GKD implementation instantiates the Guided-OPD objective in Section 3.2, so we use the same notation as the main text. Using the full-vocabulary next-token distributions at each position j∈ℳtj\in\mathcal{M}_{t}, we compute the distillation loss:

ℒOPD=1|ℳt|​∑j∈ℳtDβ​(pθ,j∥sg⁡[pT,jgt]),β=1,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}_{t}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{M}_{t}}D_{\beta}\left(p_{\theta,j}\;\middle\|\;\operatorname{sg}\left[p_{T,j}^{g_{t}}\right]\right),\qquad\beta=1,

where pθ,j=πθ(⋅∣xt,y^t,<j)p_{\theta,j}=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{t},\hat{y}_{t,<j}) is the student distribution at position jj, and pT,jgt=πT(⋅∣x~t,y^t,<j)p_{T,j}^{g_{t}}=\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid\tilde{x}_{t},\hat{y}_{t,<j}) is the teacher distribution conditioned on the most-matched guidance gtg_{t}. The operator sg⁡[⋅]\operatorname{sg}[\cdot] denotes stop-gradient. Our implementation parameterizes the generalized JSD/KL family by β\beta; with β=1\beta=1, it selects the reverse-KL direction:

D1(p∥q)=DKL(p∥q)=∑vp(v)logp⁡(v)q⁡(v).D_{1}(p\|q)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=\sum_{v}p(v)\log\frac{p(v)}{q(v)}.

Therefore, the reported experiments use full-vocabulary, per-prefix reverse KL, not a sampled-token surrogate. The teacher forward pass is executed under no_grad and its logits are detached; gradients flow only through the student distribution. One teacher-forced forward pass over the complete completion provides teacher distributions for all valid prefixes. We use sampling temperature 1.01.0 and top-p=0.98p=0.98 for student rollouts.

A.6 Reinforcement Learning with GRPO

After GKD, we further optimize the policy with group relative policy optimization (GRPO). For each logged prompt, the behavior policy samples G=16G=16 completions; candidates are scored at the same logged GUI state rather than by executing live environment transitions. Rewards are normalized within the group to form relative advantages:

A^t(i)=Rt(i)−mean⁡({Rt(j)}j=1G)std⁡({Rt(j)}j=1G)+ϵadv.\hat{A}_{t}^{(i)}=\frac{R_{t}^{(i)}-\operatorname{mean}(\{R_{t}^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{G})}{\operatorname{std}(\{R_{t}^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{G})+\epsilon_{\mathrm{adv}}}.

Here ϵadv\epsilon_{\mathrm{adv}} is a numerical stabilizer distinct from the clipping bounds below. We use sequence-level importance sampling and the clipped GRPO objective:

ℒGRPO=−1G∑i=1Gmin(ρt(i)A^t(i),clip(ρt(i),1−ϵlow,1+ϵhigh)A^t(i))+βKLDKL(πθ∥πref),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}=-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\min\left(\rho_{t}^{(i)}\hat{A}_{t}^{(i)},\,\mathrm{clip}(\rho_{t}^{(i)},1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}},1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}})\hat{A}_{t}^{(i)}\right)+\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}),

where the sequence-level importance ratio is computed from the mean token log-probability difference:

ρt(i)=exp⁡[1|ℳt(i)|​∑j∈ℳt(i)(log⁡πθ​(y^t,j(i)∣xt,y^t,<j(i))−log⁡πθold​(y^t,j(i)∣xt,y^t,<j(i)))].\rho_{t}^{(i)}=\exp\!\left[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}^{(i)}_{t}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{M}^{(i)}_{t}}\left(\log\pi_{\theta}(\hat{y}^{(i)}_{t,j}\mid x_{t},\hat{y}^{(i)}_{t,<j})-\log\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(\hat{y}^{(i)}_{t,j}\mid x_{t},\hat{y}^{(i)}_{t,<j})\right)\right].

Here ℳt(i)\mathcal{M}^{(i)}_{t} denotes the valid completion-token positions and A^t(i)\hat{A}_{t}^{(i)} is the group-normalized advantage defined in Section 3.3. The resulting scalar ratio is shared by the whole completion and is the only quantity clipped; no token-wise clipping is applied. We use ϵlow=0.2\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}}=0.2, ϵhigh=0.28\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}=0.28, dynamic sampling, and overlong-response filtering in both 2B and A3B GRPO runs. The KL coefficient is βKL=0\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}=0 for both runs.

The reward profile is local_subtask. It combines multi-solution GUI action matching, subtask quality judged by a local Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct reward model, and a JSON-aware soft overlength penalty. The reward functions and weights passed to training are:

R=0.60​Rms+0.30​Rsub+0.10​Rformat/length.R=0.60\,R_{\mathrm{ms}}+0.30\,R_{\mathrm{sub}}+0.10\,R_{\mathrm{format/length}}.

The subtask reward model is served locally with vLLM. For the 2B run, two local reward servers are used; for the A3B run, four local reward servers are used. For the A3B policy, generated outputs are additionally constrained by a structured JSON regular expression requiring fields for reasoning, subtask decomposition, and the next action. The Rformat/lengthR_{\mathrm{format/length}} term is an auxiliary output-validity regularizer, not a semantic task-success reward: malformed or schema-invalid JSON receives no format credit, while valid but overlong responses receive a soft length penalty under the completion limits listed in Table 6.

A.7 Data Pipeline

To facilitate the training of Lite-GUI, we developed a two-stage data construction pipeline consisting of an automated trajectory generation phase and a high-quality multi-solution annotation phase, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Both Lite-Dataset and Lite-Bench are generated through this pipeline.

A.7.1 Automated Trajectory Generation (Data Pipeline)

In this section, we detail the Automated Trajectory Generation (ATG) framework, a self-evolving pipeline designed to synthesize high-quality interaction trajectories for GUI agents. The framework leverages a "generation-verification-correction" closed-loop mechanism to mitigate error propagation and hallucinations in long-horizon tasks.

Multimodal Context Representation

At each discrete time step tt, the system constructs a comprehensive multimodal input 𝒳t\mathcal{X}_{t}:

𝒳t={𝒯n​a​m​e,ℐt,ℋt​e​x​t,𝒱h​i​s​t}\mathcal{X}_{t}=\{\mathcal{T}_{name},\mathcal{I}_{t},\mathcal{H}_{text},\mathcal{V}_{hist}\} (29)

where 𝒯n​a​m​e\mathcal{T}_{name} denotes the task identifier, ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} is the current RGB screenshot, ℋt​e​x​t\mathcal{H}_{text} represents the historical dialogue logs, and 𝒱h​i​s​t={ℐt−1,ℐt−2}\mathcal{V}_{hist}=\{\mathcal{I}_{t-1},\mathcal{I}_{t-2}\} provides the temporal visual context through the two preceding frames.

Decision Engine: Qwen3-VL-32B

We employ Qwen3-VL-32B as the core GUI Model to parse 𝒳t\mathcal{X}_{t} and generate a structured decision tuple 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t}:

𝒟t=⟨Reasoning, Subtasks, Action, Value, Position⟩\mathcal{D}_{t}=\langle\text{Reasoning, Subtasks, Action, Value, Position}\rangle (30)

The model explicitly outputs its cognitive chain via Reasoning and decomposes complex objectives into granular Subtasks, ensuring the logical consistency of the resulting Action and its corresponding coordinates (Position), for reference, see Fig. 7 and system prompt refers to Fig. 3.

Robust Verification and Feedback-driven Refinement

To ensure the reliability of generated actions, a peer Qwen3-VL-32B model acts as the Verify Model, for reference, see Fig. 7 and system prompt refers to Fig. 4.

Majority Voting Mechanism

For each candidate action 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t}, the Verify Model performs three independent evaluations considering task relevance and planning accuracy. An action is committed to the execution environment (PC) if and only if it secures a majority consensus:

C​o​u​n​t​(Eval="Yes")≥2Count(\text{Eval}=\text{"Yes"})\geq 2 (31)

Iterative Self-Correction and Recency-based Fallback

If the consensus threshold is not met, the framework initiates a feedback loop (up to N=3N=3 iterations):

  • •

    Feedback Injection: The Eval and Reasoning from the Verify Model are fed back into the GUI Model as negative constraints to guide policy refinement.

  • •

    Evolutionary Selection: In cases where the loop reaches the maximum iteration limit without a consensus, the system adopts a Recency-based Selection strategy. It executes the action from the latest iteration that yielded the highest number of "Yes" votes.

  • •

    Rationale: This strategy assumes that the sequential accumulation of feedback cues progressively narrows the search space, rendering the latest refined output the most robust approximation of the optimal policy.

A.7.2 Data Aggregation and Policy Enhancement

Post-execution, successful trajectories are archived into a centralized Data Pool. By integrating these synthesized trajectories with existing open-source datasets, we provide a rich, multi-domain corpus for subsequent post-training stages, including OPD and reinforcement learning, thereby continuously improving the agent’s generalization capabilities across diverse GUI environments.

Guided On-Policy Distillation and Reinforcement Learning Data Construction

The Guided On-Policy Distillation and Reinforcement Learning Data Construction phase (as illustrated in Fig. 1) serves as the core refinement engine for transforming linear explorations into high-density, multi-path expert demonstrations. This process shifts the dataset from a singular-path trajectory to a topological decision graph through state-space exploration and human-in-the-loop auditing.

  • •

    State-space Exploration and Stochastic Inference: Building upon the multi-step trajectories collected during the ATG phase, the framework performs an in-depth exploration of the state space. For any intermediate state sts_{t} within a trajectory, we employ Qwen3-VL-32B to perform multiple independent stochastic inferences. The objective is to probe the existence of alternative valid solutions for the current sub-task. By varying the decoding parameters, the model generates a set of potential candidate actions {at1,at2,…,atn}\{a_{t}^{1},a_{t}^{2},\dots,a_{t}^{n}\}, effectively uncovering the inherent strategy diversity of the GUI environment.

  • •

    Expert Auditing and Policy Refinement: The candidate actions generated during the exploration phase are mapped into a structured semantic format. These candidates are then submitted to a Manual Annotation process, which acts as the ultimate "quality gate." Expert annotators evaluate each proposed action against the visual state and task objectives. As depicted in Fig. 1, correct actions that logically advance the task are marked as "True" and preserved, while erroneous or redundant actions are pruned. This human-in-the-loop verification eliminates model hallucinations and ensures the high fidelity of the branched trajectories.

  • •

    RL Data Densification: The culmination of this process is a structured "Multi-Solution" dataset where a single task at a specific step possesses multiple validated paths. This construction significantly densifies the reward landscape for the subsequent Guided On-Policy Distillation and Reinforcement Learning stages. Rather than simple imitation learning, the agent is provided with a rich ensemble of successful strategies, fostering superior decision resilience and error-recovery capabilities.

A.8 Lite-Dataset

A.8.1 Task Domains and Environment Configuration

The Lite-Dataset is a large-scale, high-fidelity multimodal dataset specifically designed for the training and evaluation of autonomous GUI agents. The dataset is strictly rooted in a native PC terminal environment similar to Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, simulating authentic productivity workflows.

  • •

    Full-stack Productivity Ecosystem: The dataset covers low-level system management (File System, Terminal commands, and System Settings) as well as high-level professional applications, including the full WPS Office suite (Writer, Spreadsheets, and Presentation).

  • •

    Challenge Benchmarks: We have introduced complex interaction tasks involving VS Code, Dingding, and specialized interfaces for Musa Digital Human and AI Assistants. These tasks are defined as "Challenge Benchmarks," where the decision space exhibits non-linear growth as task complexity increases.

A.8.2 Standardized Action Space

To bridge the gap between high-level visual perception and system-level execution, we define a standardized action space 𝒜\mathcal{A} within the Lite-Datasets. Each action consists of a type, target coordinates (Position), and optional parameters (Value):

  • •

    Mouse Interactions: Includes CLICK, RIGHT_CLICK, DOUBLE_CLICK, DRAG, and SCROLL_UP/DOWN for page navigation and content scrolling.

  • •

    Keyboard Operations: Includes TEXT_INPUT for string entry and KEY for discrete key presses or complex combinations (e.g., CTRL+A).

  • •

    System Control: The WAIT action suspends the agent for 1 second, ensuring system stability and accounting for asynchronous loading latencies.

A.8.3 Guided On-Policy Distillation and RL Pipeline

To construct an expert demonstration library for reinforcement learning, we designed a data construction pipeline based on stochastic exploration:

  • •

    Contextual Sliding Window: Long-horizon trajectories are truncated into manageable samples with a maximum window of three steps (comprising three dialogue turns and three screenshots) to enhance the precision of local decision-making.

  • •

    Multi-Solution Stochastic Exploration: We utilize Qwen3-VL-32B to perform re-inference on the final round of each windowed sample. By increasing the temperature (T​e​m​p​e​r​a​t​u​r​e=1.0Temperature=1.0), the model performs multiple samplings (N=5N=5) to obtain diverse results, which are subsequently deduplicated and stored. The specific output format of these samples follows the template defined in Fig. 7.

  • •

    Human-in-the-loop Verification: All candidate paths generated during exploration undergo rigorous manual annotation. We constructed 30,000 complete multi-step trajectories and approximately 70,000 derived windowed training samples; across the collected data, 11,000 samples carry human-verified multi-solution annotations. Detailed examples of these multi-path ground truths can be found in Fig. 7.

A.8.4 Error-aware Trajectory Modeling

A distinguishing feature of Lite-Datasets is its inclusion of negative supervision signals. Within the complete trajectories collected via the Automated Trajectory Generation (ATG) phase, we intentionally preserved and labeled samples where human annotators identified errors in intermediate steps. This error-aware modeling provides critical negative feedback, enabling the agent to improve its error-correction capabilities and robustness in complex, real-world environments.

A.9 Lite-Bench

A.9.1 Benchmark Overview and Design Philosophy

To rigorously evaluate the multi-step complex task completion capabilities of GUI agents, we present Lite-Bench. Built upon a live Ubuntu 22.04 environment, Lite-Bench shifts the evaluation paradigm from static offline prediction to dynamic, closed-loop interaction. The benchmark is specifically designed to stress-test the agent’s core competencies in long-term planning, visual grounding, complex instruction comprehension, and error recovery within a non-stationary environment.

A.9.2 Task Composition and Procedural Constraints

Lite-Bench comprises 160 tasks, featuring 75 web tasks, 38 terminal tasks, and 47 file system tasks that strictly prohibit terminal usage to enforce pure vision-based interaction. None of the 160 Lite-Bench evaluation task instances is included in the training samples. However, some evaluation tasks share workflow families with training examples while differing in their target entities or object values. We therefore interpret Lite-Bench as an evaluation of transfer to held-out task instances, not as a task-family-disjoint test of generalization to entirely unseen workflows. To simulate the efficiency constraints of professional workflows, each task is capped at a maximum of 18 steps. The tasks are categorized into three primary domains:

  • •

    File System: Focuses on GUI-based file management, directory structuring, and visual data organization. Notably, Lite-Bench enforces a strict procedural constraint: file system tasks must be accomplished through the graphical file manager. Operations executed via the Terminal for these specific tasks are recorded as failures, ensuring the benchmark measures GUI manipulation proficiency rather than command-line scripting.

  • •

    Web Browser: Involves multi-tab navigation, semantic information retrieval, and complex web-form processing.

  • •

    Terminal: Covers standard command-line operations, system-level configurations, and environment debugging.

For a complete evaluation of this fixed task set, the pooled success rate must satisfy All=(47​File+75​Web+38​Terminal)/160\mathrm{All}=(47\,\mathrm{File}+75\,\mathrm{Web}+38\,\mathrm{Terminal})/160, up to displayed rounding. The same identity applies to an average over repeated evaluations when every run uses this task set and denominator. As stated above, OS-World and Lite-Bench results are arithmetic means over five independent runs.

A.9.3 Evaluation Protocol: LLM-as-a-Judge

The non-trivial nature of verifying GUI task success requires a nuanced understanding of both final states and interaction sequences. Lite-Bench adopts an automated "LLM-as-a-Judge" protocol utilizing the latest GPT-5.4 multimodal model:

  1. 1.

    Real-time Execution: The agent interacts with the live Ubuntu environment. Upon task completion or reaching the 18-step limit, the system automatically exports a comprehensive execution log (JSON) and a full-process trajectory of screenshots.

  2. 2.

    Multimodal Auditing: The execution artifacts are fed into GPT-5.4. The judge model is instructed to perform a dual-criteria audit:

    • •

      Outcome Verification: Does the final UI state satisfy the initial user instruction?

    • •

      Compliance Auditing: Did the agent adhere to the required interaction modality (e.g., using GUI instead of Terminal for file tasks)?

  3. 3.

    Success Rate (SR): The primary metric is the Success Rate, defined as the percentage of tasks verified as "Successful" by the judge model based on the criteria above.

By combining a live execution environment with a high-level multimodal auditing mechanism, Lite-Bench provides an objective, scalable, and challenging framework for assessing the next generation of general-purpose GUI agents.

Separately from the training-time planning judge evaluated in Appendix A.4, we calibrate the GPT-5.4 benchmark evaluator. On a held-out human-annotated subset, GPT-5.4 agrees with human judgments at 93.7% for file tasks, 93.4% for browser tasks, and 94.8% for terminal tasks, with 93.9% overall agreement. ScreenSpot-Pro is evaluated over its fixed benchmark images. For OS-World and Lite-Bench, every reported result for our models and ablations is the arithmetic mean of five independent runs; the tables do not mix single-run and repeated-run values. The repetition protocol of literature baselines is not established here.

To audit train–test independence, we compared Lite-Bench instructions with approximately 70K training samples using BGE-M3 embeddings and a similarity threshold of 0.80. Only 862 training samples exceeded the threshold, and no identical task instructions were found. Lite-Bench covers File System, Web, and Terminal, whereas Lite-Dataset spans more than seven application categories, including Feishu, AI assistants, and WPS.

A.10 Analysis of Guided On-Policy Distillation

Unless otherwise specified, all diagnostics in this section are conducted on N=50N=50 multi-solution validation states. For the student solution-coverage analysis, we sample K=8K=8 independent completions per state.

We conduct two complementary diagnostic analyses to better understand the effect of privileged guidance in Guided-OPD. The first evaluates whether privileged guidance improves the teacher’s ability to discriminate valid GUI actions from invalid ones. The second examines whether Most-Matched-GT causes the student policy to collapse toward a narrower subset of valid solutions. The results are summarized in Table 7.

Teacher-scoring diagnostic.

For each validation state ii, let aisela_{i}^{\mathrm{sel}} denote the human-verified valid action selected as privileged guidance, aiotha_{i}^{\mathrm{oth}} denote another human-verified valid action that is not provided as guidance, and ainega_{i}^{\mathrm{neg}} denote an invalid action sampled from another GUI state. Let

si​(a)∈[0,1]s_{i}(a)\in[0,1]

denote the score assigned by the same Qwen3-VL-32B teacher to candidate action aa under the corresponding teacher context.

We report five metrics to characterize teacher supervision quality.

Selected Valid. This metric measures the average teacher score assigned to the valid action selected as privileged guidance:

Ssel=1N​∑i=1Nsi​(aisel).S_{\mathrm{sel}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}s_{i}(a_{i}^{\mathrm{sel}}).

A larger value indicates that the teacher assigns higher confidence to the guidance-selected valid action.

Other Valid. To determine whether privileged guidance improves supervision beyond the explicitly provided reference, we also evaluate another human-verified valid action that is not used as guidance:

Soth=1N​∑i=1Nsi​(aioth).S_{\mathrm{oth}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}s_{i}(a_{i}^{\mathrm{oth}}).

An increase in this metric indicates that the effect of privileged guidance is not restricted to the selected reference action, but also improves the teacher’s recognition of alternative valid GUI decisions.

Invalid. We measure the average score assigned to an invalid action:

Sneg=1N​∑i=1Nsi​(aineg).S_{\mathrm{neg}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}s_{i}(a_{i}^{\mathrm{neg}}).

A lower value is preferred, as it indicates that the teacher does not assign high confidence to actions that are invalid for the current GUI state.

Valid–Invalid Margin. We measure the separation between valid and invalid actions by averaging the scores of the two valid candidates and subtracting the invalid-action score:

MV−I=Ssel+Soth2−Sneg.M_{\mathrm{V-I}}=\frac{S_{\mathrm{sel}}+S_{\mathrm{oth}}}{2}-S_{\mathrm{neg}}.

A larger margin indicates that the teacher more clearly separates valid GUI actions from invalid alternatives, yielding a more discriminative supervision signal.

Pairwise Preference Accuracy. We further measure whether the teacher ranks valid actions above the invalid action. For each state, we compare both valid candidates against the invalid candidate:

PairAcc=12​N​∑i=1N[𝕀⁡(si​(aisel)>si​(aineg))+𝕀⁡(si​(aioth)>si​(aineg))],\mathrm{PairAcc}=\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[\mathbb{I}\left(s_{i}(a_{i}^{\mathrm{sel}})>s_{i}(a_{i}^{\mathrm{neg}})\right)+\mathbb{I}\left(s_{i}(a_{i}^{\mathrm{oth}})>s_{i}(a_{i}^{\mathrm{neg}})\right)\right],

where 𝕀⁡[⋅]\mathbb{I}[\cdot] is the indicator function. A larger value means that the teacher more consistently prefers valid actions over invalid ones.

As shown in Table 7(a), Guided-OPD increases the Selected Valid score from 0.596 to 0.980 and the Other Valid score from 0.314 to 0.532, while the Invalid score remains at 0.000. Accordingly, the Valid–Invalid Margin increases from 0.455 to 0.756, and Pairwise Preference Accuracy improves from 46% to 77%. Importantly, the improvement on Other Valid indicates that privileged guidance does more than simply increase confidence in the provided reference action; it also improves the teacher’s discrimination of alternative valid GUI decisions.

Student solution-coverage diagnostic.

We next examine whether the stronger alignment introduced by Most-Matched-GT reduces the diversity of valid actions produced by the student. For each validation state ii, we independently sample K=8K=8 completions from the student policy:

a^i,1,a^i,2,…,a^i,K.\hat{a}_{i,1},\hat{a}_{i,2},\ldots,\hat{a}_{i,K}.

Let Ai∗A_{i}^{*} denote the human-verified valid-action set for state ii. A sampled action is considered valid if it matches at least one action in Ai∗A_{i}^{*} according to the GUI action-matching function. We define

mi,j=𝕀[∃a∗∈Ai∗,a^i,j∼a∗],m_{i,j}=\mathbb{I}\left[\exists a^{*}\in A_{i}^{*},\;\hat{a}_{i,j}\sim a^{*}\right],

where a^i,j∼a∗\hat{a}_{i,j}\sim a^{*} denotes that the sampled action matches the corresponding human-verified valid action.

We report three metrics to quantify valid-action reliability and solution diversity.

ValidRate@8. ValidRate@8 measures the fraction of the eight sampled actions that are valid:

ValidRate​@​8=1N​∑i=1N1K​∑j=1Kmi,j,K=8.\mathrm{ValidRate@8}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^{K}m_{i,j},\qquad K=8.

This metric measures the reliability of the student policy under repeated sampling: a larger value indicates that a greater fraction of generated actions are valid.

UniqueValid@8. For each state, we define the set of distinct human-verified valid actions recovered by the sampled outputs as

Ui={a∗∈Ai∗|∃j∈{1,…,K},a^i,j∼a∗}.U_{i}=\left\{a^{*}\in A_{i}^{*}\;\middle|\;\exists j\in\{1,\ldots,K\},\hat{a}_{i,j}\sim a^{*}\right\}.

We then compute

UniqueValid​@​8=1N​∑i=1N|Ui|.\mathrm{UniqueValid@8}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}|U_{i}|.

Unlike ValidRate@8, which can be high even when the same valid action is repeatedly generated, UniqueValid@8 measures how many distinct valid action modes are observed under repeated sampling.

Coverage@8. Coverage@8 measures the fraction of the annotated valid-action set recovered by the student samples:

Coverage​@​8=1N​∑i=1N|Ui||Ai∗|.\mathrm{Coverage@8}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{|U_{i}|}{|A_{i}^{*}|}.

A larger value indicates that the student covers a larger fraction of the human-verified valid solution space.

As shown in Table 7(b), Most-Matched-GT Guided-OPD improves ValidRate@8 from 0.5175 to 0.5725, while increasing UniqueValid@8 from 0.52 to 0.66 and Coverage@8 from 0.26 to 0.33. The final MD-GRPO model further increases ValidRate@8 to 0.6375 while preserving UniqueValid@8 and Coverage@8 at 0.66 and 0.33, respectively. These results indicate that Most-Matched-GT improves the reliability of valid-action generation without reducing the observed diversity or coverage of valid solutions.

A.11 Inference Efficiency and Training Cost

We benchmarked inference with three-window GUI contexts. On one A100, Qwen3-VL-2B reaches 103.0 tokens/s at approximately 4.5 GB VRAM, Lite-GUI-30B-A3B reaches 91.54 tokens/s at approximately 18 GB, whereas the Qwen3-VL-32B teacher reaches 27.27 tokens/s and requires two A100 GPUs with tensor parallelism. On one RTX 4090, Qwen3-VL-2B reaches 81.2 tokens/s in BF16 and Lite-GUI-30B-A3B reaches 17.7 tokens/s with AWQ; the dense 32B AWQ model runs out of memory.

The 11K multi-solution annotations required approximately 120 human hours. The full data-generation and training pipeline required approximately 1.2K A100 GPU hours. These are one-time offline costs; they trade against lower inference memory and latency for the resulting lightweight models.

Under the same controlled training configuration, the SFT baseline requires approximately 4 GPU-hours, compared with 17 GPU-hours for Most-Matched-GT-Guided-OPD. In an additional ShowUI-Desktop-8K comparison with identical model settings, SFT, Most-Matched-GT-Guided-OPD, and GRPO require approximately 0.5, 4, and 12 hours, respectively, and achieve 30.55%, 46.29%, and 43.51% ScreenSpot-Pro accuracy.

A.12 Limitations and Broader Impacts

Although our method improves GUI-agent training through guided on-policy distillation and multi-solution dual-level reinforcement learning, several limitations remain.

First, the human-verified valid action set 𝒜t∗\mathcal{A}_{t}^{*} is only a finite approximation of the full valid action space. GUI tasks often admit many semantically equivalent action paths, and our annotations cannot exhaustively cover all possible correct actions. As a result, a model output that correctly advances the task may still receive a lower reward if the corresponding action is not included in the annotated multi-solution set. The Most-Matched-GT selector should therefore be understood as an alignment heuristic that reduces supervision–state mismatch, not as a guarantee that all valid action modes remain equally represented.

Second, constructing multi-solution annotations requires additional human verification. Compared with single-action supervision, annotating and validating multiple acceptable actions for the same GUI state is more expensive and may limit scalability to new applications, operating systems, or task domains.

Third, the planning reward relies on a frozen Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct model as an external VLM judge during RL training. Although the judge is not used at inference time, it increases training cost and may introduce model-specific evaluation bias. In particular, the judge may over- or under-estimate the quality of a subtask plan when the screenshot history is ambiguous or when the plan uses a valid but uncommon strategy.

Fourth, GRPO is a practical choice for our logged-state setting rather than a claim of superiority over critic-based PPO. PPO may provide finer-grained credit assignment when reliable value targets and online rollouts are available, while our setting avoids an additional critic and the cost of repeated GUI interaction. A compute-matched GRPO–PPO comparison remains future work.

Fifth, our latency and memory measurements are server-class measurements and do not include a full energy study or a broad on-device deployment evaluation. Our experiments focus on GUI-agent tasks under the evaluated benchmark and data distribution. The results may not directly generalize to all operating systems, applications, screen resolutions, languages, or highly dynamic interfaces. Further evaluation is needed before deploying such agents in open-ended real-world environments.

Finally, GUI automation systems can have both positive and negative societal impacts. They may improve productivity and accessibility by automating repetitive computer tasks, but they may also cause unintended operations, privacy leakage from screenshots, or misuse in unauthorized automation. Practical deployment should include permission control, sensitive-action confirmation, logging, and privacy filtering for screenshot-based data.

For all existing assets, we use them only for research purposes and follow their official license and usage terms. We do not redistribute third-party pretrained models or benchmark assets with restrictive terms; instead, we provide instructions for obtaining them from their official sources when necessary. Our released assets only include our own GUI trajectories, annotations, prompts, configurations, and code components that we are permitted to distribute.
